    How to read this exhibit

    This simulator shows a simplified birdsong pathway. HVC provides the timing sequence, RA selects a pattern of downstream activity, five oscillators create control signals, and the syrinx produces sound.

    1. Click HVC or press Run song.
    2. HVC activates one or more RA ensembles through the editable HVC → RA connections.
    3. RA turns on matching oscillator channels.
    4. Vocal control combines those oscillator signals into p(t) and k(t).
    5. DM drives the respiratory system / lungs, supplying airflow and pressure to the syrinx; nXIIts provides syringeal motor control.
    6. The spectrogram on the right shows the sound energy over time and frequency.

    What this simulation uses:

    • HVC: sequential timing events.
    • RA: combinations of 5 ensembles chosen by the HVC → RA map.
    • Oscillator stage: 5 model oscillators, one for each RA ensemble.
    • Pitch control: the slider changes k(t), the model stiffness signal.
    • Dynamics noise: scales stochastic perturbations in the oscillator/vocal-control dynamics, producing rendition-to-rendition variation while keeping the HVC → RA wiring fixed.
    • Randomize connections: creates a new deterministic HVC → RA wiring and therefore a new song structure.
    • Connection editing: lets you manually redraw how HVC drives RA.
    • Node positioning: moves HVC, RA and oscillator symbols on the anatomical image without changing their existing connectivity.

    Technical Basis — Hierarchical Nonlinear Dynamics of Birdsong Generation

    This interactive exhibit is based on the generative model of Yildiz & Kiebel (2011) and its Supplementary Text S1. The framework combines sequential neuronal population dynamics in HVC, attractor dynamics in RA, RA-modulated oscillators, and a nonlinear physical model of the avian syrinx. The hierarchy is generative: the output of each level becomes the input that drives the level below.

    HVC sequence→ RA attractor state→ RA-modulated oscillators→ bounded P(t), T(t)→ syrinx dynamics→ sound / spectrogram

    1. HVC — sequential population dynamics

    HVC is represented as a continuous-time recurrent neuronal-rate network. Its inhibitory connectivity is chosen so that activity moves through a stable heteroclinic sequence: one HVC population becomes active, then the next. The example model uses eight HVC ensembles, with their output providing the time-dependent drive to RA.

    ẋ⁽³⁾ = κ₃[−λx⁽³⁾ − R S(x⁽³⁾) + 1] + ν₁⁽³⁾
    v⁽³⁾ = G(x⁽³⁾) + ν₂⁽³⁾

    Functional role: HVC supplies the temporal ordering of the song-generating sequence.

    2. RA — asymmetric attractor dynamics

    RA is modeled as a continuous-time asymmetric Hopfield-like network. Different HVC inputs drive the five-dimensional RA population toward different stable activity patterns. Supplementary Text S1 specifies the stability condition and how the HVC input vector is chosen for a desired RA attractor.

    ẋ⁽²⁾ = κ₂[−A x⁽²⁾ + W Q(x⁽²⁾) + I] + ν₁⁽²⁾
    H = (W + Wᵀ)/2,   H − A negative definite
    I = c φ(x*) − W φ(x*),   c = a / tanh(1)
    v⁽²⁾ = (x⁽²⁾ + 1)/2 + ν₂⁽²⁾    ;    w⁽²⁾ = G(x⁽²⁾) + ν₃⁽²⁾

    Under the stated condition, the RA network has a unique globally asymptotically stable equilibrium. Choosing the input vector I for a target state x* therefore lets a particular HVC ensemble select a desired RA attractor.

    3. First level — mixtures of RA-modulated oscillators

    Supplementary Text S1 gives the explicit oscillator dynamics. Each RA output vᵢ⁽²⁾ gates one oscillatory component. The normalization factor keeps the steady-state oscillation amplitude controlled, while the second state is a phase-shifted version of the first. The RA output wᵢ⁽²⁾ determines how strongly each oscillator contributes to the two lower-level outputs.

    ẋᵢ⁽¹⁾ = vᵢ⁽²⁾ √[1 + (fᵢκ₁)²] sin(fᵢκ₁t) − xᵢ⁽¹⁾ + ω₁⁽¹⁾
    ẏᵢ⁽¹⁾ = vᵢ⁽²⁾ √[1 + (fᵢκ₁)²] sin[fᵢ(κ₁t − θ)] − yᵢ⁽¹⁾ + ω₂⁽¹⁾
    v⁽¹⁾ = Σᵢ wᵢ⁽²⁾ xᵢ⁽¹⁾ + ω₃⁽¹⁾
    w⁽¹⁾ = Σᵢ wᵢ⁽²⁾ yᵢ⁽¹⁾ + ω₄⁽¹⁾
    fᵢ = i f₁,   i = 1,…,5

    If the corresponding RA ensemble is inactive, its oscillator contributes approximately zero to the final mixture. Thus RA converts a population code into a time-varying combination of oscillatory motor-control signals.

    4. Bounded neural control → bilateral syrinx

    HVC → RA oscillator mixtures generate two intermediate neural control signals, v(t) and w(t). A bounded adapter converts them into the same pressure P(t) and labial tension T(t) used by the synthetic birdsong demonstration. Both left and right syrinx states receive the same parameters.

    uP = clamp((v(t) + 0.18) / 0.80, 0, 1)
    uT = clamp((w(t) + 0.18) / 0.76 + 0.025 × pitchShift, 0, 1)
    P(t) = −0.10 + 0.35 uP   [−0.10, 0.25]
    T(t) = −0.10 + 1.10 uT   [−0.10, 1.00]
    dx/dt = y
    dy/dt = −Pγ² − Tγ²x − γ²x³ − γx²y + γ²x² − γxy

    The identical bounded controls drive two independently integrated labial states (γ = 24,000). Their sound sources are combined and filtered by the 3.5 cm trachea (reflection 0.10), followed by a Helmholtz OEC (4 kHz, Q=4).

    This mapping from neural oscillator outputs to P and T is an exhibition adapter, not a fitted physiological parameter estimate. The neural circuit and original wiring remain unchanged. Acoustic equations and the tract architecture follow the birdsong demonstration based on Amador et al. (2013) and Boari et al. (2015).

    Implementation note. The main article and Supplementary Text S1 provide the scientific hierarchy, RA stability construction, oscillator equations, and syrinx dynamics used as the basis for this exhibit. The interactive interface adds manual HVC triggering, editable or randomized HVC → RA wiring, the pitch and noise controls, visualization timing, and browser-oriented numerical scaling. These controls are intended for exploration and are not claims about additional biological mechanisms beyond the published model.
    Primary reference: Yildiz, I. B. & Kiebel, S. J. (2011). A Hierarchical Neuronal Model for Generation and Online Recognition of Birdsongs. PLoS Computational Biology, 7(12), e1002303. DOI: 10.1371/journal.pcbi.1002303.
    Supplementary source: Yildiz & Kiebel (2011), Supplementary Text S1, including RA stability conditions, the HVC-dependent attractor input construction, RA-modulated oscillator dynamics, and sensitivity analysis of connectivity matrices.
    Audio starts after a click because browsers block autoplay. For exhibition use, Chrome/Edge/Firefox with speakers or headphones works best.
